questions.stem: Which of the following is true of patients chronically infected with Helicobacter pylori primarily in the antrum?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is true of patients chronically infected with Helicobacter pylori primarily in the antrum?

options.label: B
options.text: They produce reduced amounts of acid compared to acutely infected patients.

options.label: C
options.text: They are predisposed to develop peptic ulcer disease manifested by gastric ulcers.

options.label: D
options.text: They are predisposed to develop duodenal ulcers.

questions.answerText: They are predisposed to develop duodenal ulcers.
questions.solution: Correct Option D - They are predisposed to develop duodenal ulcers: Patients infected with H. pylori are usually asymptomatic, but up to 15% develop peptic ulcer disease. Patients who have predominant antral infection are most likely to develop duodenal ulcers. Incorrect Options: Option A - They manifest pangastritis primarily: Most patients (85%) chronically infected with H. pylori have pangastritis. Option B - They produce reduced amounts of acid compared to acutely infected patients: Patients with antral predominant infection with H. pylori have reduced antral somatostatin secretion and content and subsequently produce increased amounts of acid. Patients with acute infection produce increased somatostatin and decreased gastrin and acid. Option C - They are predisposed to develop peptic ulcer disease manifested by gastric ulcers: Patients with antral predominant infection are most likely to develop duodenal ulcers. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 70-year-old female patient presents for evaluation of scleral icterus that she noted a week ago and dull abdominal pain that has become persistent over the last month. Past medical history is significant for hypertension. Vital signs are within normal limits, and physical exam is significant for tenderness to palpation in the epigastrium without rebound or guarding. Her labs reveal total bilirubin 7 mg/dL with amylase 110 U/L. USG abdomen shows extrahepatic biliary dilation. CT reveals a hypoattenuated 3 cm density consistent with pancreatic adenocarcinoma with no evidence of spread. The tumor appears to abut the celiac artery. What is the best option for the evaluation and management of this patient?

CT reveals a hypoattenuated 3 cm density consistent with pancreatic adenocarcinoma with no evidence of spread. The tumor appears to abut the celiac artery. What is the best option for the evaluation and management of this patient?

questions.solution: Correct Option C - EUS: Endoscopic ultrasound is indicated to determine the extent of invasion and for biopsy confirmation of the diagnosis. EUS-guided FNA is less likely to result in intraperitoneal spread of the tumor compared to percutaneous biopsy and has a sensitivity of approximately 90% for diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. EUS may be more accurate than CT for defining the relationship of the tumor to the vasculature. Resectability criteria include clear planes around the celiac, hepatic, and superior mesenteric arteries and no distortion of the portal vein or superior mesenteric vein. Incorrect Options: Option A - PET scan to rule out distant metastatic disease: In this case, there is no evidence of intraabdominal spread on CT. An assessment of resectability can be derived from triple phase staging contrast-enhanced CT and EUS is the preferred modality for tissue diagnosis. Option B - ERCP with stent: ERCP is useful for detection of extrahepatic biliary obstruction. Compared to CT, it is invasive, associated with complications and a mortality rate of 0.2%, and is also costlier. It is indicated for therapy in patients with cholestasis due to obstruction of the biliary system by tumor for placement of a biliary stent. If a pancreatic carcinoma is potentially resectable, stenting is not indicated prior to resection in the absence of cholangitis. Option D - Surgical consult for resection: Histological diagnosis is indicated and EUS will also assist with the determination of resectability by defining the relationship of the tumor to the vasculature. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following cognitive assessment tools is commonly used to assess various cognitive domains, including memory, attention, and language, in geriatric medicine?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following cognitive assessment tools is commonly used to assess various cognitive domains, including memory, attention, and language, in geriatric medicine?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - MoCA, which stands for Montreal Cognitive Assessment: MoCA is a widely used cognitive assessment tool in geriatric medicine. It assesses various cognitive domains, including memory, attention, language, and visuospatial abilities, providing a more comprehensive evaluation of cognitive function in older adults. Incorrect Options: Option A - MMSE (Mini-Mental State Examination): The MMSE is another common cognitive screening tool, but it has limitations compared to the MoCA in assessing a wide range of cognitive domains. Option C - CAM (Confusion Assessment Model): CAM is a tool used to assess delirium, not a comprehensive cognitive assessment in geriatric medicine. Option D - PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire-9): The PHQ-9 is a questionnaire used to assess depression symptoms, not cognitive function. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient with a history of myasthenia gravis is hospitalized in the intensive care unit for a myasthenic crisis. Due to worsening respiratory weakness, the patient required intubation and mechanical ventilation. On day 3 of hospitalization, the patient develops ventilator-associated pneumonia. Tracheobronchial aspiration reveals infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which of the following antibiotics is absolutely contraindicated for this patient?
questions.stemHtml:
A 35-year-old patient with a history of myasthenia gravis is hospitalized in the intensive care unit for a myasthenic crisis. Due to worsening respiratory weakness, the patient required intubation and mechanical ventilation. On day 3 of hospitalization, the patient develops ventilator-associated pneumonia. Tracheobronchial aspiration reveals infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Which of the following antibiotics is absolutely contraindicated for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D – Gentamicin: Neuromuscular blockade is a rare and serious side effect that can occur with aminoglycosides. Thus, the use of aminoglycosides is absolutely contraindicated in patients with myasthenia gravis. Aminoglycosides are useful in the treatment of many aerobic gram-negative and gram-positive organisms and are frequently used in combination with other antibiotics. Although neuromuscular blockade is a possible side effect, the most common toxicities include nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Incorrect Options: Option A - Meropenem: Meropenem is a carbapenem antibiotic. Its main contraindications are hypersensitivity to it or other carbapenems or a history of anaphylaxis to beta-lactams. Option B - Ceftazidime: It is a third-generation cephalosporin. Contraindications include previously documented hypersensitivity to cephalosporins, penicillins, or beta-lactam antibiotics. Option C - Aztreonam: It is not absolutely contraindicated in patients with myasthenia gravis. Common side effects include neutropenia and increased liver enzymes. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: You review a 25-year-old man in the clinic who has a diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia which was diagnosed at the age of 9. He takes dexamethasone 0.25 mg daily. Which of the following is the best investigation to monitor a patient with classic salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)?
questions.stemHtml: You review a 25-year-old man in the clinic who has a diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia which was diagnosed at the age of 9. He takes dexamethasone 0.25 mg daily. Which of the following is the best investigation to monitor a patient with classic salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - 17 hydroxyprogesterone (17 OHP) levels: Classic salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder with a prevalence of 1: 10,000 - 1: 15,000. It is due to a deficiency of 21 alpha-hydroxylase enzyme and usually presents with an acute life-threatening illness in a neonate with vomiting, dehydration, circulatory collapse and features of adrenal insufficiency on biochemistry but can also present later in life. Management includes steroid replacement and about 3/4th of patients may require mineralocorticoid replacement in addition. Monitoring of treatment is based on clinical examination (signs of hyperandrogenism and glucocorticoid excess) and biochemical measurement of 17 OHP levels. Renin activity may also be used to monitor the adequacy of replacement with associated mineralocorticoid deficiency - patient would be on fludrocortisone. Incorrect Options: Option B - 21 alpha hydroxylase: This is not a common investigation for monitoring CAH. The deficiency in 21-hydroxylase is what characterizes CAH, and measuring this enzyme's levels is not a standard monitoring approach. Option C - DHEA levels: While DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) is involved in adrenal steroid synthesis, it is not as specific or sensitive as 17 OHP in monitoring classic salt-wasting CAH. Option D - Measure plasma renin activity: While measuring plasma renin activity can provide information about the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and may be relevant in some cases of CAH, it is not as specific or primary a marker for monitoring classic salt-wasting CAH as 17 OHP levels. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presented to the emergency department with shock, pulsatile abdominal mass and severe mid-abdomen pain. Open repair of the ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm was done. What would be the 30-day mortality rate for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man presented to the emergency department with shock, pulsatile abdominal mass and severe mid-abdomen pain. Open repair of the ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm was done. What would be the 30-day mortality rate for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- 50%: The 30-day mortality rate in patients who underwent open surgical repair of the ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is 50%. Most patients with ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysms do not survive to reach the hospital. If the patient survives and reaches the hospital, there should be no delay in clamping the aorta. Open repair is the treatment of choice in emergency situations, and a Dacron graft replaces the aneurysmal segment. Incorrect Options: Option A- 100%: The 30-day mortality rate is not 100% in this patient. A patient who survives the ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm and reaches the hospital, and survives the operation has a long-term survival approaching that of a normal population. Option B- 10-20%: The 30-day mortality rate in patients who underwent open surgical repair of the ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is not 10-20%. 10-20% is the 30-day mortality rate in patients who underwent emergency open surgical repair for symptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm. Option D- 5-8%: 5-8% is the 30-day mortality rate in patients who underwent elective open surgical repair for asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysms. 5-8% is inconsistent with the 30-day mortality rate in patients who underwent emergency surgical repair for ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D- Aspirin: An antiplatelet drug called aspirin is frequently employed in treating acute coronary syndromes, including NSTEMI. It functions by preventing platelet activation, which aids in preventing the development of blood clots in the coronary arteries. Incorrect Options: Option A- Nitroglycerin: Nitroglycerin is used to treat chest pain because of NSTEMI. However, it does not play a part in averting subsequent cardiac episodes. Option C- Metoprolol: Metoprolol is a beta blocker that can help to reduce heart rate and blood pressure in patients with NSTEMI but is not as effective as antiplatelet therapy in preventing further cardiac events. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the ER with increasing fatigue, difficulty breathing, easy bruising, and now acute gum bleeding. An initial CBC shows a WBC of 90,000 109/L, a plt count of 15000/mm3, and a Hgb 7.2 g/dL. A peripheral smear shows large, immature appearing granulocytes with bright pink granules and large bilobed nuclei that appear creased. Based on the clinical presentation and smear data above, which of the following is the most important treatment to initiate emergently?
questions.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman presents to the ER with increasing fatigue, difficulty breathing, easy bruising, and now acute gum bleeding. An initial CBC shows a WBC of 90,000 109/L, a plt count of 15000/mm3, and a Hgb 7.2 g/dL. A peripheral smear shows large, immature appearing granulocytes with bright pink granules and large bilobed nuclei that appear creased. Based on the clinical presentation and smear data above, which of the following is the most important treatment to initiate emergently?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - All-trans retinoic acid: The patient's presentation of acute fatigue, difficulty breathing, easy bruising, gum bleeding, and the peripheral smear showing large, immature granulocytes with bright pink granules and large bilobed nuclei that appear creased is highly suggestive of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). APL is associated with a coagulopathy that can lead to life-threatening bleeding complications. The most important treatment to initiate emergently in a suspected case of APL is all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA). ATRA is a key component of APL therapy and can induce differentiation of the malignant promyelocytes, leading to a reduction in the coagulopathy and a rapid improvement in symptoms. Starting ATRA as soon as possible is critical to prevent and manage the potentially fatal bleeding complications associated with APL. Incorrect Options: Option A- Transfusion of PRBCs: While transfusion of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) may be necessary to address the anemia in APL, it does not directly address the underlying disease process or the coagulopathy associated with APL. ATRA is the primary treatment to initiate urgently. Option B- Idarubicin: Idarubicin is a chemotherapy agent often used in the treatment of AML, including APL. However, in the context of APL, all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) is typically initiated first to rapidly improve the coagulopathy. Once the patient's condition is stabilized, further treatment options can be considered. Option D- Arsenic: Arsenic trioxide (ATO) is an effective treatment for APL and is often used in combination with ATRA. However, in an emergent situation like this, ATRA is usually started before confirmatory diagnostic results are obtained due to its rapid impact on the coagulopathy. ATO and ATRA are often used in consolidation and maintenance phases of APL treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following proteins is responsible for fast anterograde axonal transport?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following proteins is responsible for fast anterograde axonal transport?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Kinesin: Two force-generating ATPases named kinesin and dynein are responsible for fast anterograde and fast retrograde axonal transport, respectively. An important function of anterograde axonal transport is to ship proteins made in the cell body down to the presynaptic terminal, whereas retrograde axonal transport plays a role in returning membrane molecules to the cell body for processing and elimination and in communication between the presynaptic terminal and the cell body. questions.stem: A 32 year old female G3P3 with a h/o multiple uterine fibroids induced DUB after uterine artery embolization is transfused with RBCs. During the transfusion she develops nausea, chills, rigors, and mild dyspnea. Her temperature is 38.4 ° C. Work-up for hemolysis is negative. How should this patient be managed?
questions.stemHtml: A 32 year old female G3P3 with a h/o multiple uterine fibroids induced DUB after uterine artery embolization is transfused with RBCs. During the transfusion she develops nausea, chills, rigors, and mild dyspnea. Her temperature is 38.4 ° C. Work-up for hemolysis is negative. How should this patient be managed?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Acetaminophen: This patient's presentation is most consistent with a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR). Appropriately named, patients present with a fever (a temperature rise > 1°C) without hemolysis after a transfusion. FNHTR is common and can occur during or ~1 to 6 hours after a transfusion of red cells or platelets. Additional symptoms can include headache, nausea, vomiting, chills, rigors, mild dyspnea, and hypotension. Patients are managed with reassurance, acetaminophen (an antipyretic), and occasionally meperidine (for rigors). Incorrect Options: Option A - Lasix: Lasix (furosemide) is a loop diuretic commonly used to treat fluid retention. It would not be the appropriate choice for managing febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions (FNHTR), which are characterized by fever, chills, and rigors, rather than fluid overload. Option C - Epinephrine, Benadryl, and Corticosteroids: This combination of medications is used to manage severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, during transfusion. Anaphylaxis presents with more severe symptoms such as difficulty breathing, hypotension, and potentially life-threatening symptoms. The patient's symptoms in this scenario (fever, chills, rigors, mild dyspnea) are more consistent with FNHTR, not anaphylaxis. Option D - Supportive Care and Ventilatory Support: Supportive care and ventilatory support are indeed the management options for transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), which presents with acute respiratory distress, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and hypoxemia. However, these symptoms are not present in the given patient's case. The patient's symptoms of fever, chills, rigors, and mild dyspnea are more indicative of FNHTR. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 32-year-old male with a smoking history presents with cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. On examination, he has bilateral crackles in his lungs and decreased urine output. A chest X-ray shows diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and urinalysis reveals microscopic hematuria. A renal biopsy is performed, and the pathology report shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old male with a smoking history presents with cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. On examination, he has bilateral crackles in his lungs and decreased urine output. A chest X-ray shows diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and urinalysis reveals microscopic hematuria. A renal biopsy is performed, and the pathology report shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Goodpasture syndrome: This patient's clinical presentation, with hemoptysis, diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and renal involvement, raises suspicion of an autoimmune disease affecting both organs. Goodpasture syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of autoantibodies against type IV collagen, a component of the glomerular and alveolar basement membrane. The most common presentation is acute kidney injury with pulmonary hemorrhage. The diagnosis is made by demonstrating the presence of anti-GBM antibodies or by showing linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane on renal biopsy. In this patient, the renal biopsy showed linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane, confirming the diagnosis of Goodpasture syndrome. The presence of pulmonary hemorrhage on imaging and hemoptysis further supports this diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Option A- Wegener's granulomatosis: Option A (Wegener's granulomatosis) is an autoimmune disease that affects small blood vessels and can involve the kidneys, lungs, and upper respiratory tract. While the clinical presentation of hemoptysis and pulmonary infiltrates may be similar to Goodpasture syndrome, the histopathology findings are different. In Wegener's granulomatosis, the characteristic histopathological feature is necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, not linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane. Therefore, option A is an incorrect answer in this scenario. Option C- Sarcoidosis: Option C (Sarcoidosis) is a multisystem inflammatory disease affecting the lungs, skin, eyes, and other organs. The hallmark histopathological feature of sarcoidosis is non-caseating granulomas, not linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane. While sarcoidosis can present with pulmonary infiltrates and renal involvement, the presence of linear IgG and C3 deposition on renal biopsy is not consistent with this diagnosis. Therefore, option C is an incorrect answer in this scenario. Option D- Alport syndrome: Option D (Alport syndrome) is a genetic disorder that affects the glomerular basement membrane and can cause kidney disease and hearing loss. While it can present with hematuria, the presence of pulmonary infiltrates, hemoptysis, and linear IgG and C3 deposition on renal biopsy is not consistent with this diagnosis. Therefore, option D is an incorrect answer in this scenario. @Neet_pg_bot

A person is considered contagious 4 days before and after the onset of rash. It is important to be aware of measles infection due to the recent outbreak in the United States. Valsartan is used to manage his hypertension. He has smoked a single pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. Cardiac auscultation reveals normal heart sounds; there are no murmurs or rubs. questions.solution: Correct Option A- Oral Atenolol: The signs and symptoms of this patient suggest a stable coronary artery disease (CAD). Stable coronary artery disease is a type of coronary artery disease in which there are pathological atherosclerotic changes in the coronary vessel walls. Patients are either asymptomatic or have stable or low-risk unstable angina with normal ECG and normal cardiac markers. It is also used to characterize patients with a previous myocardial infarction whose symptoms are controlled with treatment. A first-line treatment for individuals with stable CAD, Atenolol , is a beta 1-selective adrenergic receptor blocker that improves exercise tolerance and decreases the frequency of anginal episodes. Like other beta-blockers, Atenolol lowers heart rate and cardiac contractility, lowering myocardial oxygen demand and alleviating anginal discomfort. The rise in coronary vascular resistance that results from beta-blockers inhibition of adrenergic-mediated coronary vasodilation is offset by the lower heart rate, which increases coronary perfusion by lengthening diastole. Risk-reducing measures (secondary prevention of CAD) include weight reduction, quitting smoking, aerobic exercise, and pharmaceutical treatment (which includes antiplatelet therapy, lipid-lowering therapy, and management of hypertension and diabetes). If there are contraindications to beta-blockers or if beta-blockers do not sufficiently manage symptoms, alternative antianginal agents are calcium channel blockers, long-acting nitrates (such as isosorbide mononitrate), and ranolazine. Incorrect Options: Option B- low dose aspirin: Aspirin inhibits COX-1 irreversibly , which prevents platelet aggregation. Antiplatelet therapy lowers the chance of complications from stable angina (e.g., myocardial infarction). It is recommended for all patients with ischemic heart disease who do not have particular contraindications to antiplatelet drugs. However, aspirin therapy does not improve exercise tolerance or decrease anginal pain in patients with stable angina. Option C- Percutaneous coronary angiography: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is typically used to diagnose and manage the acute coronary syndrome. In stable angina, as seen here, PCI is only indicated if there are activity-limiting symptoms despite optimal medical treatment, contraindications to medical therapy, or stenosis of multiple coronary arteries (e.g., left coronary artery), none of which are present in this patient. Option D- Sublingual nitroglycerin: To increase coronary perfusion and lower cardiac oxygen demand, nitroglycerin , a short-acting nitrate, dilates the coronary vasculature and lowers left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (preload). In individuals with stable ischemic heart disease , it may decrease anginal symptoms. Nitroglycerin is a first-line treatment for alleviating acute angina symptoms but does not increase endurance during prolonged activity. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is admitted to the intensive care unit. The patient requires mechanical ventilation. Which of the following parameters should be closely monitored to prevent ventilator-associated lung injury (VALI)?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old patient with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is admitted to the intensive care unit. The patient requires mechanical ventilation. Which of the following parameters should be closely monitored to prevent ventilator-associated lung injury (VALI)?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Peak Inspiratory Pressure (PIP): Monitoring Peak Inspiratory Pressure (PIP) is crucial in preventing ventilator-associated lung injury (VALI) in mechanically ventilated patients, especially in those with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). PIP represents the maximum pressure reached during each ventilator-assisted breath and can provide valuable information about the potential for lung overdistention and barotrauma. Incorrect Options: Option B - Fraction of Inspired Oxygen (FiO 2 ): FiO 2 represents the concentration of oxygen delivered to the patient and is adjusted to maintain adequate oxygenation. While it is essential to optimize oxygenation, monitoring FiO2 alone may not prevent VALI, which is primarily related to ventilatory pressures and volumes. Option C - Tidal Volume (TV): Tidal volume refers to the volume of air delivered with each breath. In patients with ARDS, using a lower tidal volume (6-8 mL/kg of predicted body weight) is recommended to prevent VALI. However, monitoring TV alone may not be sufficient to prevent lung injury; PIP should also be closely monitored to ensure that the set tidal volume is not causing excessive pressures. Option D - Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP): PEEP is used to recruit collapsed alveoli and improve oxygenation in ARDS. It plays a crucial role in preventing atelectasis and maintaining functional residual capacity (FRC). While monitoring PEEP is important, it primarily affects oxygenation and lung recruitment rather than directly preventing VALI. The risk of VALI is more closely associated with PIP. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - Peak Inspiratory Pressure (PIP):

  • Monitoring Peak Inspiratory Pressure (PIP) is crucial in preventing ventilator-associated lung injury (VALI) in mechanically ventilated patients, especially in those with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). PIP represents the maximum pressure reached during each ventilator-assisted breath and can provide valuable information about the potential for lung overdistention and barotrauma.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Fraction of Inspired Oxygen (FiO2): FiO2 represents the concentration of oxygen delivered to the patient and is adjusted to maintain adequate oxygenation. While it is essential to optimize oxygenation, monitoring FiO2 alone may not prevent VALI, which is primarily related to ventilatory pressures and volumes.

Option C - Tidal Volume (TV): Tidal volume refers to the volume of air delivered with each breath. In patients with ARDS, using a lower tidal volume (6-8 mL/kg of predicted body weight) is recommended to prevent VALI. However, monitoring TV alone may not be sufficient to prevent lung injury; PIP should also be closely monitored to ensure that the set tidal volume is not causing excessive pressures.

Option D - Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP): PEEP is used to recruit collapsed alveoli and improve oxygenation in ARDS. It plays a crucial role in preventing atelectasis and maintaining functional residual capacity (FRC). While monitoring PEEP is important, it primarily affects oxygenation and lung recruitment rather than directly preventing VALI. The risk of VALI is more closely associated with PIP.

questions.stemHtml: What drug FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis has also been shown to dampen downbeat nystagmus leading to significant symptom relief in some patients?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - 4-aminopyridine : 4-aminopyridine (Ampyra or dalfampridine) is a potassium channel blocker that is FDA-approved to help improve gait in multiple sclerosis patients. It has been shown in several smaller studies to subjectively improve oscillopsia and objectively reduce nystagmus amplitude on eye movement tracings in patients with downbeat nystagmus. The proposed mechanism of action is that 4-AP prolongs the after-polarization of the action potential and improves Purkinje cell pacemaker function in DBN patients. Incorrect Options: Option B - Fingolimod: Fingolimod is an oral medication used in the treatment of relapsing forms of MS. It works by modulating the immune system. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Doxycycline: This patient is pregnant and PCN allergic with neurologic manifestations of lyme disease and she likely has early disseminated Lyme disease. Although tetracyclines are generally avoided in pregnancy, doxycycline rather than a second-line agent (eg, azithromycin) has been shown to be safe when a short course is required. questions.stem: Which of the following is characteristic of graft vs. host disease after transfusion or transplantation?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is characteristic of graft vs. host disease after transfusion or transplantation?

options.label: A
options.text: Host T lymphocytes attack the donor tissue

options.label: B
options.text: It is most common in the first week after allogeneic stem cell transplantation

options.label: C
options.text: Steroids are effective in over 95% of patients

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Cholestatic hyperbilirubinemia is common: Graft vs. host disease can occur after transfusion or any allogenic transplant, including bone marrow, stem cell, or tissue transplant from a donor to another individual. It results from the response of T lymphocytes from the allogeneic donor to host antigens. It is most common during the second month after allogeneic hemopoietic cell transplant, occurring in up to 66% of patients. Patients experience nausea, abdominal pain, secretory diarrhea, GI bleeding from mucosal ulcerations, a maculopapular rash, and/or cholestatic hyperbilirubinemia. Liver biopsy is usually precluded by thrombocytopenia. Severe disease is associated with poor prognosis. Treatments include steroids, anti-TNF, and photopheresis, but they are not consistently effective. Incorrect Options: Option A - Host T lymphocytes attack the donor tissue: Donor T lymphocytes attack host tissue. Option B - It is most common in the second month after allogeneic hemopoietic cell transplantation: The degree of severity is associated with the degree of HLA dissimilarity between recipient and donor tissue. Option C - Steroids are effective in over 95% of patients: Treatments available include steroids, but no treatment is consistently effective. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Continue midostaurin for up to 1 year with CBC checks every 1-2 months: The use of midostaurin, especially in combination with standard chemotherapy, has shown to improve outcomes in patients with FLT3-mutated AML. Given that the patient has completed intensive chemotherapy and is in remission, continuing midostaurin serves as maintenance therapy to reduce the risk of relapse. Monitoring with CBC checks every 1-2 months is necessary to watch for any signs of relapse or complications. Incorrect Options: Option A- Discontinue midostaurin and referral back for transplantation: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation can be an effective treatment for patients with FLT3-mutated AML, especially if they have a high risk of relapse. However, in the given scenario, the patient is in remission after consolidation therapy. Simply discontinuing midostaurin and referring for transplant without evidence of relapse may expose the patient to the risks of transplantation without clear benefit. Option B- Discontinue midostaurin and monitor with complete blood count every 3-4 weeks While monitoring with CBC is essential, discontinuing midostaurin when the patient is in remission might risk an early relapse. Maintenance therapy with midostaurin can help prolong the duration of remission. questions.answerText: 600 mL volume, low calorie meal ingested by mouth
questions.solution: Correct Option A - 600 mL volume, low calorie meal ingested by mouth: Volume of food ingested suppresses hunger and stimulates the sense of fullness more than the calorie content of the meal. Typically, the average volume of water ingested to achieve fullness is 600 mL. Also, it has been shown that nutrients taken by mouth suppress hunger greater than infusion of nutrients into the stomach or duodenum. Postprandial fullness is not completely understood physiologically but is believed to be due, in large part, to stretching on the stomach walls and secretion of gastric juices. Incorrect Options: Option B - 300 mL volume, high calorie meal ingested by mouth: This option is incorrect because a high-calorie meal is more likely to stimulate hunger and appetite in normal individuals compared to a low-calorie meal. Option C - 600 mL volume, low calorie meal ingested directly via PEG tube: This option is incorrect because hunger suppression is not solely dependent on the volume of the meal. In this case, ingesting the meal via a PEG tube may not provide the same sensory and hormonal cues as oral ingestion, potentially leading to less hunger suppression. Option D - 300 mL volume, low calorie meal ingested by mouth: This option is incorrect because it involves a lower volume and lower calorie intake, which is less likely to suppress hunger in normal individuals compared to option A. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Volume depletion: In this patient with 2 days of fluid loss due to possible food poisoning, volume depletion is almost certain Polycythemia is defined as an abnormally elevated hemoglobin or hematocrit. It can be classified as relative polycythemia (spuriously elevated due to volume depletion) or absolute polycythemia (accompanied by an increased red blood cell mass). Patients with relative polycythemia often have a clinical history and physical examination consistent with volume depletion as well as a normal red blood cell mass. Treatment involves volume repletion and addressing the underlying cause. Absolute polycythemia may be caused by an increased production of red blood cells (primary polycythemia) or by a response to increased erythropoietin leading to an increased red blood cell mass (secondary polycythemia). The anticoagulant effect of warfarin is mediated via which of the following mechanisms of action?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman has atrial fibrillation and a CHADS2-VASc score of 3. She has been on warfarin and asks about newer alternatives to warfarin that she has seen advertised on television. In the course of your discussion she asks how warfarin "thins her blood." The anticoagulant effect of warfarin is mediated via which of the following mechanisms of action?

options.label: A
options.text: ADP antagonist at the P2Y12 receptor

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Vitamin K epoxide reductase inhibition: Warfarin inhibits the production of vitamin K-dependent proteins within the coagulation cascade including factors II, VII, IX, X, and the anticoagulant proteins C and S. Warfarin specifically inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase and therefore inhibits the recycling of vitamin K. As warfarin has no effect on vitamin K-dependent proteins that are already synthesized, the onset of action is delayed by 3-4 days after initiation (time required for normal breakdown of previously synthesized clotting factors and their replacement by the deficient factors processed in the presence of warfarin). Given that proteins C and S are natural anticoagulants, and protein C has a very short half-life, warfarin can therefore create a transient hypercoagulable state soon after its initiation. Incorrect Options: Option A - ADP antagonist at the P2Y12 receptor: This mechanism of action is associated with antiplatelet medications like Clopidogrel (Plavix), not warfarin. These drugs inhibit ADP-induced platelet activation and aggregation. Option C - Cyclooxygenase inhibition: This mechanism is associated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as aspirin, but it is not the mechanism of action of warfarin. Option D - Direct factor Xa inhibition: Factor Xa inhibitors like rivaroxaban (Xarelto) and apixaban (Eliquis) directly inhibit factor Xa, a key component in the coagulation cascade. This is a newer class of anticoagulant medications, but it is not the mechanism of action of warfarin. Option E - Direct thrombin inhibition: Thrombin inhibitors like dabigatran (Pradaxa) directly inhibit thrombin, which is an enzyme involved in the coagulation process. Again, this is a newer class of anticoagulant drugs but not the mechanism of action of warfarin. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 38-year-old female, otherwise in good health, was driving with relatives when their vehicle got stuck in the sand. Later, the relatives found her unresponsive in the van. As she was pulled out, a strong smell of fumes was noticed. The paramedics noticed agitation and intubated her in the field. In less than 2 hours, the patient is taken to the ER of the nearby hospital. The oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximeter is 100% on 100 percent oxygen. She is sedated. Her temperature is 98.0°F, pulse is 88/min, and BP is 121/86 mm of Hg. A co-oximeter measured carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hb) level is 26%, and hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy is considered. Which biochemical measurement is suggested as a marker of severity of poisoning?

Her temperature is 98.0°F, pulse is 88/min, and BP is 121/86 mm of Hg. A co-oximeter measured carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hb) level is 26%, and hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy is considered. Which biochemical measurement is suggested as a marker of severity of poisoning?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Lactate: CO-Hgb levels are likely positively correlated with initial lactate levels in carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. Patients who received HBO treatment had elevated plasma lactate concentrations and additionally had more frequent altered mental status. Although HBO therapy is used in different settings, generally accepted indications for HBO treatment are the presence of significantly increased COHb values and neurologic or cardiac deterioration. However, a lactate value >1.85mmol/L can predict the need for HBO treatment, which could be taken as a measure of severe poisoning. Lactate levels are also increased in alcohol intoxication, salicylate poisoning, and paraquat poisoning. Incorrect Options: Option B - Carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hgb): While carboxyhemoglobin levels are measured to confirm carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning and guide treatment decisions, it is not considered a marker of the severity of poisoning. CO-Hgb levels indicate the percentage of hemoglobin that is bound to carbon monoxide instead of oxygen. A high CO-Hgb level, as in this case (26%), confirms the diagnosis of CO poisoning, but it does not provide information about the severity of the poisoning or the degree of tissue hypoxia. The severity of CO poisoning is better assessed by clinical features, such as the patient's mental status, oxygen saturation, and the presence of symptoms like confusion, agitation, or altered consciousness. Option C - Creatinine: Creatinine levels are not used as a marker of severity in carbon monoxide poisoning. Creatinine is a waste product produced by muscles and excreted by the kidneys. It is commonly measured to assess kidney function and to estimate glomerular filtration rate (GFR). In cases of carbon monoxide poisoning, the focus is on assessing the extent of tissue hypoxia and damage caused by the lack of oxygen, rather than kidney function. Option D - Creatine phosphokinase (CrPK or CPK): Creatine phosphokinase (also known as creatine kinase or CPK) is an enzyme found in various tissues, including muscle and brain cells. Elevated CPK levels can indicate muscle damage, such as in muscle injuries, heart attacks, or rhabdomyolysis. However, CPK levels are not used as a marker of severity in carbon monoxide poisoning. The focus in CO poisoning is primarily on evaluating the extent of tissue hypoxia and its effects on the brain and other organs @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male with refractory B-cell acute lymphoid leukemia (B-ALL, dx 6 months ago) is currently on ECOG 1910 regimen. He has atrial fibrillation on Lovenox and a history of pulmonary embolism. He is admitted to the ICU with acute neutropenic septic shock secondary to klebsiella bacteremia. There are no other associated symptoms like chest pain, cough, nausea, vomiting, rash, or headache. However, he reports 1-2 days of diarrhea. The decision is made to intubate due to an inability to compensate adequately for severe metabolic acidosis due to suspected gut translocation. Echocardiogram shows mildly dilated LA. LVEF is 60%. He has no valvular abnormalities and normal ventricular contractility. Chest X-ray shows increasing airspace opacities, bilateral lung bases, and midzone alveolar edema. Pneumonia is excluded. The patient has a persistent, small left pleural effusion with associated slight basal atelectasis. Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is considered. As per the Berlin criteria, which oxygenation would label the ARDS as mild?

options.label: A

questions.answerText: 200 < PaO2/FiO2 ≤ 300 with PEEP or CPAP ≥5cm H2O
questions.solution: Correct Option A - 200 < PaO 2 /FiO 2 ≤ 300 with PEEP or CPAP ≥5cm H 2 O: The severity of ARDS is classified into 3 mutually exclusive categories of ARDS based on the degree of hypoxemia: mild (200 mmHg < PaO 2 /FIO 2 ≤ 300 mmHg), moderate (100 mmHg < PaO 2 /FIO 2 ≤ 200 mmHg), and severe (PaO 2 /FIO 2 ≤ 100 mmHg), all with PEEP or CPAP ≥5cm H 2 O. Using the Berlin definition, stages of mild, moderate, and severe ARDS are associated with increased mortality (27%; 95% CI, 24%-30%; 32%; 95% CI, 29%-34%; and 45%; 95% CI, 42%-48%, respectively; P <0.001) and increased median duration of mechanical ventilation in survivors (5 days; interquartile [IQR], 2-11; 7 days; IQR, 4-14; and 9 days; IQR, 5-17, respectively; P <0.001). Compared to the American-European Consensus Conference (AECC definition), the final Berlin definition had better predictive validity for mortality. Incorrect Options: Option B - 100 < PaO 2 /FiO 2 ≤ 200 with PEEP or CPAP ≥5cm H 2 O: This option corresponds to moderate ARDS (100 < PaO 2 /FiO 2 ≤ 200 with PEEP or CPAP ≥5cm H 2 O). In moderate ARDS, the patient's oxygenation index is lower, indicating more severe hypoxemia compared to mild ARDS. Option C - PaO 2 /FiO 2 < 100 with PEEP or CPAP ≥5cm H 2 O: This option corresponds to severe ARDS (PaO 2 /FiO 2 < 100 with PEEP or CPAP ≥5cm H 2 O). In severe ARDS, the patient's oxygenation index is even lower, indicating the most severe form of hypoxemia among the three categories. Option D - 200 < PaO 2 /FiO 2 ≤ 300 with PEEP or CPAP ≥10cm H 2 O: This option corresponds to moderate ARDS (200 < PaO 2 /FiO 2 ≤ 300 with PEEP or CPAP ≥10cm H 2 O). While the level of PEEP or CPAP is higher in this option compared to option A, it still falls under the category of moderate ARDS based on the patient's oxygenation index. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - ERCP: This patient has evidence of gallstone pancreatitis and cholangitis. Gallstones are likely to be the etiology of pancreatitis in patients with elevation of ALT. A serum ALT elevation of approximately 3x the upper limit of normal has a positive predictive value of 95% for the diagnosis of gallstone pancreatitis in this setting. Right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice are the classic presentation of acute cholangitis. Fever and abdominal pain are seen in up to 80% of patients, but jaundice is less common and is seen in up to 70%. Hypotension and mental status changes occur in more severe disease. The diagnosis should be considered in a patient with fever and/or rigors and laboratory evidence of inflammatory response in addition to either jaundice or abnormal liver chemistries. A definitive diagnosis is made when these criteria are met in the presence of biliary dilation on imaging or in the presence of evidence of an etiology such as a stone. Blood cultures should be obtained before treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics. The treatment of choice is ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy for stone extraction or insertion of a stent to establish biliary drainage. Incorrect Options: Option A - HIDA scan: There is no indication of cholecystitis, so HIDA is not indicated. Option B - Abdominal CT for evaluation of infectious necrosis: Pancreatic necrosis typically occurs later than a week after onset of acute pancreatitis. Option C - IV antibiotics and cholecystectomy: Cholecystectomy is not indicated. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Allogeneic stem cell transplant: Aplastic anaemia is a clinical syndrome caused by decreased bone marrow haematopoiesis resulting in pancytopenia. Diagnosis of aplastic anaemia requires presence of anaemia (Hb <10 gm/dL), neutropenia (neutrophil count of <1500/uL), thrombocytopenia (platelet count <50,000/uL) and absolute reticulocytopenia (reticulocyte <40,000/uL) accompanied by a hypocellular marrow without fibrosis or malignant cells. questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male presents to your clinic complaining of fatigue and malaise. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated serum creatinine levels. Based on this information, which stage of chronic kidney disease (CKD) does the patient fall under?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Stage 3: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive and irreversible condition characterized by gradually losing kidney function over time. CKD is classified into five stages based on the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and the presence of albuminuria. The five stages of CKD are as follows: Stage 1 is characterized by normal or mildly reduced eGFR (≥90 mL/min/1.73m²) with or without albuminuria. At this stage, the kidneys still function normally, and there may be no symptoms or physical signs of kidney damage. Stage 2 is characterized by mildly to moderately reduced eGFR (60-89 mL/min/1.73m²) with or without albuminuria. At this stage, there may be some mild symptoms of kidney damage, such as changes in urination, but kidney function is still fairly normal. Stage 3: This stage is characterized by moderately reduced eGFR (30-59 mL/min/1.73m²) with or without albuminuria (as in this patient with an eGFR of 35mL/min/1.73m²). Kidney function is significantly reduced at this stage, and symptoms such as fatigue, fluid retention, and anemia may occur. Stage 4 is characterized by severely reduced eGFR (15-29 mL/min/1.73m²) with or without albuminuria. At this stage, kidney function is very low, and patients may experience symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and confusion. Stage 5: This stage is also known as an end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and is characterized by severely reduced eGFR (<15 mL/min/1.73m²) with or without albuminuria. At this stage, the kidneys have lost almost all their function, and patients may require dialysis or a kidney transplant to survive. Overall, the staging of CKD is important for determining appropriate treatment options and predicting the long-term prognosis of the disease. Regular monitoring and management of CKD can help slow the progression of the disease and improve outcomes for affected individuals. questions.solution: Correct Option C- Chronic alcohol abuse: A known risk factor for the onset of myocarditis is chronic alcohol usage. questions.solution: Correct Option A- Adjuvant chemotherapy +/- radiation therapy: Uterine sarcomas account for less than 5% of uterine malignancies. Carcinosarcoma (or MMMT) was previously thought to be the most common uterine sarcoma, but is now categorized as high grade metaplastic carcinoma (and therefore classified as epithelial carcinoma). Histologic subtypes of uterine sarcomas include: Leiomyosarcoma (most common) Endometrial stromal sarcoma Undifferentiated sarcoma A new FIGO staging system for uterine sarcomas, distinct from uterine carcinoma staging, took effect in 2010. For medically operable disease, total abdominal hysterectomy/bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH/BSO) is the initial treatment of choice. According to current NCCN guidelines, the recommended adjuvant treatment approach in patients with Stage IB, II, III, IV carcinosarcoma of the uterus includes chemotherapy +/- external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) +/- vaginal brachytherapy. Although current NCCN guidelines, lumps serous carcinoma, clear cell carcinoma, and carcinosarcoma of the uterus within a single treatment category. It is important to note some granularity between these disease subtypes Given these importance differences, they remark in their conclusion "There exists a wide variation in practice and outcomes for high-risk histotypes of endometrial cancer. The relative impact of adjuvant therapy appears to be histotype dependent and prospective studies examining adjuvant treatment in high-risk histotypes should use caution combining them together." Incorrect Options: Option B - Adjuvant External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT): Radiation therapy might be considered as part of the treatment strategy, particularly if there are specific characteristics of the tumor that indicate the need for localized radiation. However, given the aggressive nature of carcinosarcoma, systemic chemotherapy is typically an essential component of treatment. Option C - Adjuvant Hormone Therapy: Hormone therapy is not typically used as the primary treatment for carcinosarcoma. This type of cancer is generally more resistant to hormonal treatments. Option D - Observation: Observation alone is not recommended for FIGO stage II carcinosarcoma. This aggressive subtype and higher stage necessitate a more active treatment approach to address potential residual disease and reduce the risk of recurrence. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Thawed fresh frozen plasma: Hemophilia A is characterized by deficiency or dysfunction of clotting factor VIII (FVIII). Patients with hemophilia A are at risk of bleeding and require FVIII replacement therapy to control bleeding episodes. In this case, the patient has an active UGI bleed with a low hemoglobin level, and FVIII replacement is urgently needed. Thawed fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is least appropriate for transfusion in this patient. Thawed FFP is FFP that has been thawed and subsequently stored at refrigerator temperature (1-6°C). It retains its clotting factors, including factor VIII (FVIII), but the activity of FVIII decreases over time, leading to reduced effectiveness in managing bleeding in hemophilia A patients. Incorrect Options: Option B - Fresh frozen plasma: Fresh frozen plasma is an appropriate choice for FVIII replacement in hemophilia A patients. It contains normal levels of clotting factors, including FVIII, and can effectively manage bleeding episodes. Option C - Cryoprecipitate: Cryoprecipitate contains high concentrations of clotting factors, including FVIII, and is commonly used for FVIII replacement in hemophilia A patients. Option D - Activated prothrombin complex: Activated prothrombin complex concentrates (aPCC) are specifically designed to provide rapid and effective FVIII replacement in hemophilia A patients with inhibitors. While they may be used, they are not the first-line choice for hemophilia A patients without inhibitors. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Start oseltamivir, call in sick, and stay home until the fever abates
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Start oseltamivir, call in sick, and stay home until the fever abates: Influenza is highly contagious. The current recommendation is antiviral therapy for individuals with suspected or confirmed influenza in the setting of any illness requiring hospitalization, progressive/severe/complicated illness, age ≥65 years, pregnant women and women up to two weeks postpartum (including those who have had pregnancy loss), and Individuals with certain medical conditions including diabetes. Incorrect Options: Option A - Start oseltamivir and go to work: Starting oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is a reasonable step if you suspect you have influenza, as it is an antiviral medication that can help reduce the severity and duration of symptoms if taken early in the course of the illness. However, going to work while experiencing influenza-like symptoms is not recommended, as influenza is highly contagious, and you could easily spread the virus to your coworkers. Going to work in this condition would not only put your colleagues at risk of getting sick but could also worsen your own condition and delay your recovery. Option C - Do not start medication and go to work: Choosing not to start oseltamivir and still going to work while experiencing symptoms of influenza is not advisable. Influenza is a contagious respiratory illness that can spread easily from person to person, especially in close settings like workplaces. By not taking antiviral medication, you are not addressing the underlying cause of your symptoms, and you risk exposing your coworkers to the virus, which could lead to a workplace outbreak. Option D - Go to work and wear a face mask: Wearing a face mask may provide some level of protection to others if you have influenza, as it can help contain respiratory droplets that may carry the virus. However, it is not a substitute for staying home when you are sick. Even with a face mask, there is still a risk of spreading the virus to others, especially if you are in close proximity to coworkers or if you touch shared surfaces without proper hand hygiene. Additionally, wearing a face mask for an extended period can be uncomfortable and may not be practical for long hours at work. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 69-year-old male presents with progressive confusion, impaired cognition, and lethargy. Neuroimaging has been unremarkable. EEG monitoring would be helpful for identifying which of the following conditions?
questions.stemHtml: A 69-year-old male presents with progressive confusion, impaired cognition, and lethargy. Neuroimaging has been unremarkable. EEG monitoring would be helpful for identifying which of the following conditions?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: Bilateral synchronous paroxysmal EEG discharges are seen in diseases diffusely affecting subcortical grey matter, but not disease states that predominantly involve grey matter. This group of subcortical grey matter involvement includes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, and herpes simplex encephalitis. Incorrect Options: Option B - Hepatic coma: Triphasic waves on EEG were historically associated with hepatic encephalopathy, also known as hepatic coma. These waves were considered a characteristic EEG finding in this condition. However, it's now known that triphasic waves can be present in various metabolic and encephalopathic conditions, and they are not specific to hepatic coma alone. While hepatic coma may present with altered mental status and impaired cognition, the presence of triphasic waves on EEG does not exclusively indicate hepatic encephalopathy. Option C - Organic solvent toxic encephalopathy: Organic solvent toxic encephalopathy can indeed cause encephalopathy and cognitive impairment due to exposure to certain chemicals or organic solvents. However, EEG findings in this condition are generally non-specific and can vary widely depending on the severity and extent of brain involvement. EEG might show diffuse slowing or other non-specific abnormalities, but there are no characteristic EEG patterns specific to organic solvent toxic encephalopathy. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Addison's disease: The clinical picture of this patient is suggestive of Addison's disease which is the most common cause of Chronic Primary Adrenal Insufficiency in developed nations. Addison's disease is a condition where the adrenal glands do not produce enough cortisol and sometimes aldosterone. The clinical features of Addison's disease include: Fatigue and weakness: One of the most common symptoms of Addison's disease is fatigue, weakness, and malaise. Patients may feel tired even after getting enough rest. Weight loss and decreased appetite: Patients with Addison's disease may experience weight loss and decreased appetite. Hyperpigmentation: This is the darkening of the skin, most commonly seen on the face, neck, and hands. It is caused by an increase in melanin production because melano cortical stimulating hormone (MSH) is produced along with adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from pro-opiomelanocortin. Hypotension: Low blood pressure due to sodium loss and iso-osmotic water loss is a common feature of Addison's disease. Patients may feel dizzy or faint when they stand up. Salt cravings: Patients may experience salt cravings due to the low aldosterone levels which results in sodium loss. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea: These symptoms may occur due to the body's inability to regulate electrolyte balance and water. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Angelman syndrome is typically caused by a paternally inherited deletion of the UBE3A gene: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon that involves the differential expression of genes depending on whether they are inherited from the mother or the father. The patient never smoked and is also seeking treatment with a hepatologist for liver issues. On examination, a prolonged wheeze is appreciated. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor which is synthesised by the liver. It inactivates the neutrophil elastase and protects the lung tissue. It is caused by a genetic mutation which causes a conformational change in the structure of alpha-1 antitrypsin. The dysfunctional protein affects the liver by accumulating in the hepatocytes' endoplasmic reticulum resulting in hepatitis and liver cirrhosis. In the lungs, its deficiency results in an uninhibited activity of neutrophil elastase, which causes pulmonary parenchyma destruction and results in pan acinar emphysema. Patients are < 60 years of age. Incorrect Options: Option B - Smoking Nicotine and smoking cause the inactivation of protease inhibitors and form reactive oxygen species. Smoking results in the destruction of respiratory bronchioles, resulting in centrilobular emphysema. Option C - Bullae formation In giant bullous emphysema, large bullae are formed, which cause the destruction of surrounding pulmonary tissue. Option D - Scar formation The chronic inflammation results in scar formation due to quartz exposure which results in cicatricial emphysema. @Neet_pg_bot

  • In giant bullous emphysema, large bullae are formed, which cause the destruction of surrounding pulmonary tissue.

Cardiac exam is unremarkable except for tachycardia. Abdomen is soft and non-tender. He has no lower extremity edema. What hemodynamic changes occur during inspiration compared to expiration in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, increased left ventricular preload, increased left ventricular afterload

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, decreased left ventricular preload, increased left ventricular afterload
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, decreased left ventricular preload, increased left ventricular afterload: The patient is in the midst of an asthma exacerbation. Because of increased airways resistance, he is requiring much wider swings in pleural pressure to get air in and out of his lungs, as manifested by his supraclavicular retractions. These intensified swings in pleural pressure result in hemodynamic changes that ultimately lead to pulsus paradoxus, a condition with significant variation in systolic blood pressure in relation to the respiratory cycle. During inspiration, pleural pressure is negative, which results in negative intrathoracic pressure. Negative intrathoracic pressure decreases the right atrial pressure, resulting in increased venous return to the right side of the heart and increased right ventricular preload. With more negative intrathoracic pressure, there is less “squeezing” of the pulmonary vasculature and more blood can remain in the pulmonary vasculature, resulting in an increase in pulmonary capacitance. Increased abdominal pressure also raises the gradient for systemic venous return. The net effect of increased abdominal pressure in the presence of normo‐ or hypervolemia is an increased systemic venous return. Because of increased right ventricular preload, the right ventricular size will increase, causing a bulge of the intraventricular septum into the left ventricle, reducing the ability of the left ventricle to fill properly, resulting in a decrease in left ventricular preload. Left ventricular preload is also reduced because more blood is staying in the pulmonary vasculature instead of entering the left side of the heart in increased pulmonary capacitance. Left ventricular afterload is defined as the amount of work that the left ventricle has to do to eject blood. If intrathoracic pressure is decreased, there is less assistance from the pressure outside of the left ventricle to squeeze the left heart to eject blood; therefore, the left ventricle has to work harder by increasing wall stress to eject blood, which increasing left ventricular afterload. Note that positive intrathoracic pressure actually reduces left ventricular afterload, and positive intrathoracic pressure “squeezes” the left ventricle, assisting it to eject blood and reducing the amount of work it has to do. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, increased left ventricular preload, increased left ventricular afterload: During an asthma exacerbation, left ventricular preload actually decreases. This is due to the increased pulmonary capacitance (more blood remaining in the pulmonary vasculature) and because of the septal shift caused by increased right ventricular preload. The septal shift reduces the ability of the left ventricle to fill properly, leading to decreased left ventricular preload. Option C - Decreased right ventricular preload, decreased pulmonary capacitance, increased left ventricular preload, decreased left ventricular afterload: Right ventricular preload and pulmonary capacitance increase, not decrease, during an asthma exacerbation due to negative intrathoracic pressure, which results from the increased effort to inhale against constricted airways. This leads to a greater volume of blood returning to the right side of the heart (increased right ventricular preload) and more blood remaining in the pulmonary vasculature (increased pulmonary capacitance). Additionally, left ventricular afterload increases, not decreases, during inspiration because the heart has to work harder to eject blood when intrathoracic pressure decreases. Option D - Increased right ventricular preload, increased pulmonary capacitance, decreased left ventricular preload, decreased left ventricular afterload: Although it correctly identifies the changes in preload and pulmonary capacitance, it incorrectly suggests that left ventricular afterload decreases. As mentioned, during inspiration, left ventricular afterload actually increases. The heart has to work harder to eject blood due to the decreased intrathoracic pressure, thereby increasing left ventricular afterload. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Abdominal CT scan: The clinical presentation of abdominal pain, acute drop in hemoglobin, and a history of pancreatic pseudocyst should raise the suspicion of a pseudoaneurysm. If emergent upper endoscopy is negative, an emergent CT scan with IV contrast should be done (preferably without oral contrast) Incorrect Options: Option A - Technetium-99m–labeled red blood cell scan: Technetium- 99m–labeled red blood cell scan and capsule study would be indicated for evaluation of obscure GI bleeding. Option B - Angiography: Positive findings of a pseudoaneurysm should be followed immediately by angiography and embolization. Option D - Capsule small bowel study: Capsule small bowel study involves the patient swallowing a small capsule containing a camera that captures images as it passes through the gastrointestinal tract. While this test can be helpful in evaluating the small bowel for sources of bleeding, it is less likely to identify the specific cause of gastrointestinal bleeding related to chronic pancreatitis. questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient presents to the clinic with complaints of facial flushing, itching, and warmth after taking a new medication for hyperlipidemia. The patient's medical history is significant for hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and obesity. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old patient presents to the clinic with complaints of facial flushing, itching, and warmth after taking a new medication for hyperlipidemia. The patient's medical history is significant for hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and obesity. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Niacin: Niacin is used in the treatment of hyperlipidemia and can cause facial flushing, itching, and warmth. Mechanism of action of niacin: Niacin works by inhibiting hormone-sensitive lipase , an enzyme involved in the breakdown of triglycerides in adipose tissue. By inhibiting this enzyme, niacin decreases the release of free fatty acids from adipose tissue, which reduces the liver's synthesis of VLDL and ultimately lowers the level of LDL cholesterol in the bloodstream. Side effects of niacin: Flushing and itching: Flushing occurs due to the release of prostaglandins, which cause vasodilation and increased blood flow to the skin. This results in the characteristic redness, warmth, and itching of the skin commonly associated with niacin use. Flushing can be prevented by taking NSAIDs 30 minutes before niacin. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, which can reduce the severity of flushing. Hepatotoxicity Hyperglycemia Hyperuricemia Diarrhoea Abdominal pain Incorrect Options: Option A- Simvastatin: Simvastatin is used in the treatment of hypercholesterolemia. Simvastatin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme that catalyses the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, which is a precursor for cholesterol synthesis. Side effects include hepatotoxicity, myalgia, myopathy, and rhabdomyolysis. Simvastatin does not cause facial flushing and itching. Option B- Alirocumab: Alirocumab is a PCSK9 inhibitor, which blocks the breakdown of LDL receptors in the liver, resulting in increased LDL removal from the bloodstream. Side effects of PCSK9 inhibitors include myalgia, delirium, and dementia. PCSK9 inhibitors do not cause facial flushing and itching. Option C- Cholestyramine: Cholestyramine is a bile acid resin that binds to bile acids in the intestine, preventing their reabsorption and promoting the excretion of bile acids. Side effects of bile acid resins include myalgia, bloating , and abdominal cramps. Bile acid resins do not cause facial flushing and itching. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 1-year-old girl was brought to a primary care physician because of a 2-days history of fever and crying while passing urine. She was diagnosed with a defect in the vesicoureteric junction with mild ureteral dilation after her first episode of febrile urinary tract infection (UTI) 3 months ago. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this condition?
questions.stemHtml:
A 1-year-old girl was brought to a primary care physician because of a 2-days history of fever and crying while passing urine. She was diagnosed with a defect in the vesicoureteric junction with mild ureteral dilation after her first episode of febrile urinary tract infection (UTI) 3 months ago.
Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Long-term prophylactic antibiotic therapy The medical treatment depends on the presence or absence of febrile UTI, age and grade of VUR. Younger age and lower VUR grade (1-3) do not generally require surgical intervention and are managed conservatively. Long-term medical treatment with prophylactic antibiotic therapy in children has been shown to decrease the risk of recurrent urinary tract infections and long-term complications, including pyelonephritis, renal scarring and chronic kidney failure. For children upto 6 weeks Ampicillin Amoxicillin Children age > 6 weeks TMP- SMX (trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole VUR with febrile UTI is associated with high morbidity; therefore, it should be managed with antibiotic prophylaxis. Indications for medical therapy: Vesicoureteral reflux grades 1-3 Unilateral Grade IV – VUR Age < 5 years Children > 3 months: Nitrofurantoin, cephalosporins, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Infants < 2 months: amoxicillin Incorrect options: Option A: Observation Observation without antibiotic prophylaxis in a patient with recurrent urinary tract infections secondary to VUR has been shown to increase the risk of pyelonephritis and renal scarring. Option B: Endoscopic injection Endoscopic injection is a surgical technique to treat VUR; however, it is usually reserved for VUR ≥ grade IV. Bilateral grade III VUR, especially in children > 6 years Worsening renal function/breakthrough urinary tract infections despite prophylactic antibiotics. Option C: Ureteral reimplantation Surgical interventions like ureteral intervention are reserved for VUR ≥ grade IV and cases unresponsive to conservative management. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Long-term medical treatment with prophylactic antibiotic therapy in children has been shown to decrease the risk of recurrent urinary tract infections and long-term complications, including pyelonephritis, renal scarring and chronic kidney failure.
  • For children upto 6 weeks
    • Ampicillin
    • Amoxicillin
  • Children age > 6 weeks
    • TMP- SMX (trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole
  • VUR with febrile UTI is associated with high morbidity; therefore, it should be managed with antibiotic prophylaxis.

Indications for medical therapy:

  • Vesicoureteral reflux grades 1-3
  • Unilateral Grade IV – VUR
  • Age < 5 years
  • Children > 3 months: Nitrofurantoin, cephalosporins, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.
  • Infants  < 2 months: amoxicillin

Option A: Observation

  • Observation without antibiotic prophylaxis in a patient with recurrent urinary tract infections secondary to VUR has been shown to increase the risk of pyelonephritis and renal scarring.

Option B: Endoscopic injection

  • Endoscopic injection is a surgical technique to treat VUR; however, it is usually reserved for VUR ≥ grade IV.
  • Bilateral grade III VUR, especially in children > 6 years 
  • Worsening renal function/breakthrough urinary tract infections despite prophylactic antibiotics.

Option C: Ureteral reimplantation

  • Surgical interventions like ureteral intervention are reserved for VUR ≥ grade IV and cases unresponsive to conservative management.

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Urodynamics: The patient’s voiding dysfunction may be related to BPH and outlet obstruction, diabetic cystopathy with poor sensation and detrusor function, or both. questions.stem: A 60-year-old shipbuilding industry worker presents to the clinic complaining of dyspnea and a non-productive cough for the last two months. Chest x-ray reveals parenchymal infiltrates in the lower lobes of the lung. A high-resolution CT scan shows ground-glass opacities and calcified pleural plaques. Exposure to which of the following substance is responsible for this pathology?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old shipbuilding industry worker presents to the clinic complaining of dyspnea and a non-productive cough for the last two months. Chest x-ray reveals parenchymal infiltrates in the lower lobes of the lung. A high-resolution CT scan shows ground-glass opacities and calcified pleural plaques. Exposure to which of the following substance is responsible for this pathology?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Asbestos: Ground-glass opacities, calcified pleural plaques, and a history of working in shipbuilding suggest a diagnosis of asbestosis. Asbestosis is an interstitial lung disease caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers. Individuals working in shipbuilding, insulation, roofing, mining, and firefighting equipment manufacturing industries are at risk of inhaling asbestos fibres. Asbestosis develops slowly over time. The clinical features of asbestosis may not become apparent until 15-20 years or more after the initial exposure to asbestos fibers. Clinical features of asbestosis include the following: Dry cough Dyspnea Weight loss Clubbing Diagnosis of asbestosis is based on the following tests: Pulmonary function test (PFT): Restrictive pattern (decreased FEV1 and normal or increased FEV1/FVC) would be seen on PFTs. Chest x-ray: Parenchymal infiltrates in the lower lobes of the lungs and pleural plaques can be seen on the chest x-ray. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT): HRCT is a more sensitive imaging test than a chest x-ray for diagnosing asbestosis. questions.stem: A 50-year-old male patient is seen with increased urination and severe thirst. Low specific gravity and low osmolality are seen in urine analyses. A lesion in the hypothalamus is visible on brain MRI. Which of the following are the patient's symptoms most likely caused?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old male patient is seen with increased urination and severe thirst. Low specific gravity and low osmolality are seen in urine analyses. A lesion in the hypothalamus is visible on brain MRI. Which of the following are the patient's symptoms most likely caused?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Decreased production of ADH: Diabetes insipidus is likely the cause of the patient's symptoms of excessive thirst and increased urine, as well as low specific gravity and low osmolality on urinalysis (DI). DI, also known as vasopressin deficit, is a condition of water balance characterised by a lack of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). The posterior pituitary gland releases ADH, which is made by the hypothalamus. Its main function is to control the body's water balance by boosting kidney water reabsorption, which lowers urine production and raises urine concentration. The kidneys cannot concentrate urine when someone has DI because of a deficit in ADH. While a result, as the body works to eliminate the extra water, there is an increase in urination and excessive thirst. The two most frequent causes of DI are nephrogenic and central, respectively. Nephrogenic DI results from a malfunction in the kidney's reaction to ADH. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increased production of ADH: Option A implies that the patient's ADH production has increased, which is false because this is the opposite of what is happening in the central DI. The posterior pituitary gland releases ADH, made by the hypothalamus, in reaction to a drop in plasma volume or an increase in plasma osmolality. Its main function is to control the body's water balance by boosting kidney water reabsorption, which lowers urine production and raises urine concentration. Option C - Increased secretion of aldosterone: A condition known as SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), characterised by excessive ADH synthesis despite normal plasma volume and osmolality, is one example where ADH production is increased. SIADH may be brought on by several illnesses, including lung disorders, cancers, or drugs. Option D - Decreased secretion of aldosterone: Aldosterone is not involved in the control of water balance. The hormone aldosterone, made by the adrenal glands, is to control the electrolyte balance by enhancing sodium and water absorption and potassium excretion in the kidneys. Aldosterone deficit leads to increased sodium and water excretion and decreased potassium excretion in conditions where aldosterone secretion is low, such as Addison's disease. @Neet_pg_bot
