questions.stem: A 35 year old patient k/c/o severe hemophilia A, who sustained a head trauma was brought by his family to the ER. The patient has been complaining of nausea and queasiness ever since the injury. CT scan of the head does not reveal any evidence of a bleed. He has not been on prophylactic replacement therapy. What would you recommend?
questions.stemHtml: A 35 year old patient k/c/o severe hemophilia A, who sustained a head trauma was brought by his family to the ER. The patient has been complaining of nausea and queasiness ever since the injury. CT scan of the head does not reveal any evidence of a bleed. He has not been on prophylactic replacement therapy. What would you recommend?

options.label: A
options.text: Observation with repeat CT head in 6 hours

options.label: B
options.text: Brain MRI with and without contrast

options.label: C
options.text: Initiate factor replacement with a target activity of 100%

questions.answerText: Initiate factor replacement with a target activity of 100%
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Initiate factor replacement with a target activity of 100%: Patients with severe hemophilia A who sustain head trauma are at a high risk of intracerebral hemorrhage (bleeding within the brain). Intracerebral hemorrhage in hemophilia patients can be life-threatening, and immediate treatment is crucial to prevent further bleeding and complications. The goal of treatment in this scenario is to raise the patient's factor VIII activity level to 100% to ensure adequate hemostasis. Factor VIII replacement therapy is the appropriate treatment option to achieve this goal. The recommended dose can be 50 IU/kg every 8-12 hours for 2 weeks. Incorrect Options: Option A - Observation with repeat CT head in 6 hours: Waiting for 6 hours and repeating a CT scan is not the appropriate course of action when a patient with severe hemophilia A presents with head trauma and symptoms like nausea and queasiness. Delaying treatment in such cases can lead to further bleeding and worsening of the patient's condition. Option B - Brain MRI with and without contrast: While brain MRI may provide detailed imaging of the brain, it is not the primary immediate intervention for a patient with severe hemophilia A who has sustained head trauma and is at risk of intracerebral hemorrhage. The priority is to initiate factor replacement therapy to control bleeding before considering additional imaging studies. Option D - FEIBA: FEIBA (Factor Eight Inhibitor Bypassing Activity) is a prothrombin complex concentrate used to manage bleeding episodes in patients with hemophilia A who have developed inhibitors (neutralizing antibodies) to factor VIII. In this case, where the patient does not have inhibitors but has head trauma and is at risk of intracerebral hemorrhage, the primary treatment is factor VIII replacement therapy to raise factor levels to 100%. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: In the lumbar region, transforaminal injections are generally preferred over interlaminar and caudal epidural injections
questions.solution: Correct Option C - In the lumbar region, transforaminal injections are generally preferred over interlaminar and caudal epidural injections: Radicular pain is a common clinical problem, especially in the lumbar spine. Studies suggest that there is both a mechanical and an inflammatory component contributing to pain production in this condition which is basis for targeted injection of corticosteroids as a therapeutic modality. In the lumbar region, there is less evidence of benefit from interlaminar and caudal epidural injections compared to transforaminal injections which are preferred in this region. Interlaminar and caudal epidural injections can still be used if the transforaminal route is not feasible for example due to anatomic limitations. Incorrect Options: Option A - Epidural injections are considered first line therapy for treatment of radicular pain and radiculopathy: Conservative therapy is still considered the first line treatment for radicular pain. Epidural injections should be reserved for who have failed a trial of conservative treatment. Option B - There is better evidence supporting epidural injections as a therapeutic procedure in the cervical spine than in the lumbar spine: The evidence for epidural injections as a therapeutic procedure is much better for their use in the lumbar region than in the cervical or thoracic region. Option D - A protocol of weekly injections for at least 3 weeks is recommended as most patients require multiple injections to demonstrate symptomatic benefit: Scheduled frequent injections are not supported by literature and should not be routinely performed. A decision to repeat an injection should be based on an individual patient’s response. Option E - Possible complications of epidural injections include allergy to the medications, radiation exposure, dural puncture, needle injury to nerves and blood vessels and, rarely, spinal cord infarction. questions.solution: Correct Option B – Increased: The PPV of a screening test represents the probability that a patient with a positive screening result does in fact have the disease in question. The PPV incorporates the prevalence of the disease, and increases with a greater prevalence within a population. Incorrect Options: Option A - Decreased: The positive predictive value (PPV) is influenced by the prevalence of the disease in the population being tested. When the prevalence of the disease decreases, the number of true positive cases will also decrease, relative to the number of false positive cases. As a result, the PPV will decrease. This is because a lower prevalence means a higher likelihood of false positive results compared to true positive results in the tested population. Option C - No change : The PPV is directly affected by the prevalence of the disease. As the prevalence changes, the PPV will also change. If the prevalence increases, the PPV will increase, and if the prevalence decreases, the PPV will decrease. Therefore, the PPV is not constant and will change with alterations in the prevalence of the disease. Option D - Not enough information to determine: There is sufficient information to determine the effect of an increase in disease prevalence on the PPV. The PPV is a mathematical metric that depends on the number of true positive cases, false positive cases, true negative cases, and false negative cases, as well as the prevalence of the disease. Given this information, we can determine the effect of changes in prevalence on the PPV. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following best characterizes restrictive lung diseases, such as pulmonary fibrosis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best characterizes restrictive lung diseases, such as pulmonary fibrosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased

options.label: B
options.text: The FEV1.0 is reduced much more than the FVC, giving a low FEV/FVC%

options.label: C
options.text: Reduction of the forced expiratory flow rate, or FEF 25-75%

options.label: D
options.text: The total lung capacity is increased to about 120%

questions.answerText: Both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased: In restrictive lung disease, such as pulmonary fibrosis, both FEV and FVC are reduced, but characteristically the FEV1.0/FVC% is normal or increased. Additional characteristics of restrictive lung disease include a total lung capacity which will be around 4 L or less. Incorrect Options: Option B - The FEV 1.0 is reduced much more than the FVC, giving a low FEV/FVC%: This characteristic is typical of obstructive lung diseases, not restrictive lung diseases like pulmonary fibrosis. In obstructive lung diseases, such as bronchial asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the airways are narrowed, leading to increased resistance to airflow. This results in a greater reduction in the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1.0) compared to the forced vital capacity (FVC). As a result, the FEV1.0/FVC% ratio is reduced, often below the normal range. Option C - Reduction of the forced expiratory flow rate, or FEF 25-75%: The reduction of the forced expiratory flow rate between 25% and 75% of the FVC (FEF25-75%) is not a characteristic feature of restrictive lung diseases like pulmonary fibrosis. Instead, it is more commonly seen in obstructive lung diseases, where there is narrowing of the airways and reduced flow rates during the mid-portion of forced expiration. It can be an early indicator of early-stage COPD before other lung function indicators, such as FEV1.0, become abnormal. Option D - The total lung capacity is increased to about 120%: An increased total lung capacity to about 120% (around 6 liters) is a characteristic finding in obstructive lung diseases, not in restrictive lung diseases. In obstructive lung diseases, the increased total lung capacity is due to air trapping caused by difficulty in fully exhaling air from the lungs, leading to a higher volume of air remaining in the lungs after exhalation. In restrictive lung diseases, like pulmonary fibrosis, the total lung capacity is reduced to around 4 liters or less due to the limited expansion of the lungs caused by the fibrotic changes in the lung tissue. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male reports to his physician with shortness of breath, wheezing, and worsening dyspnea on exertion. He also admits smoking (over 3 packs of cigarettes per day for the past 42 years). He was never intubated but has been admitted several times for acute management of COPD with bronchodilators. Physical examination reveals poor air movement in the lungs. Chest radiograph shows flattening of the diaphragm and an increased anterior-posterior chest diameter. He undergoes pulmonary function testing. Which of the following patterns will be seen on his pulmonary function tests?

He also admits smoking (over 3 packs of cigarettes per day for the past 42 years). He was never intubated but has been admitted several times for acute management of COPD with bronchodilators. Physical examination reveals poor air movement in the lungs. Chest radiograph shows flattening of the diaphragm and an increased anterior-posterior chest diameter. He undergoes pulmonary function testing. Which of the following patterns will be seen on his pulmonary function tests?

options.label: C
options.text: Normal forced expiratory volume in 1 sec/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC)

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Reduced FEV1/FVC: The forced expiratory volume in 1 second/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) is a ratio that is effort dependent and responds positively to increased expiratory effort. FEV1 is the volume of air forcefully expired with each breath during the first second. FVC is the maximal volume of air expelled with deep expiration. Residual volume (RV) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a maximal expiratory effort. Vital capacity (VC) is the maximal volume of air that may be expelled from the lungs following a maximal inspiration. A reduced FEV1/FVC is suggestive of obstructive airway disease. The reduced ratio implies decreased airway emptying because of air trapping. This patient probably has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) from smoking. Correct Options: Option A - Decreased Residual Volume/Total Lung Capacity (RV/TLC): In patients with obstructive lung diseases like COPD, the RV/TLC ratio is typically increased rather than decreased. This is because air trapping occurs in the lungs, leading to an increase in residual volume while the total lung capacity remains relatively unchanged. Option B - Decreased RV: As mentioned earlier, patients with obstructive lung diseases like COPD experience air trapping, which leads to an increase in residual volume (RV) rather than a decrease. Option C - Normal Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 sec/Forced Vital Capacity (FEV1/FVC): In a healthy individual, the FEV1/FVC ratio is typically around 70-80%. A normal ratio does not indicate the presence of obstructive airway disease. In this patient with a history of smoking, the most likely finding would be a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio due to the development of COPD. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presents with fatigue, edema, and significant proteinuria. Laboratory tests show a serum albumin level of 2.5 g/dL and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 8.0 g/g. Kidney biopsy reveals diffuse foot process effacement on electron microscopy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male presents with fatigue, edema, and significant proteinuria. Laboratory tests show a serum albumin level of 2.5 g/dL and a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 8.0 g/g. Kidney biopsy reveals diffuse foot process effacement on electron microscopy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Minimal change disease: The clinical presentation of this patient is consistent with nephrotic syndrome, as indicated by the significant proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema. Kidney biopsy findings of diffuse foot process effacement are characteristic of minimal change disease, which is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and accounts for around 20% of cases in adults. This disease is so named because it typically shows no abnormal findings on light microscopy, with only effacement of the podocyte foot processes visible on electron microscopy. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis , membranous nephropathy, and IgA nephropathy are all potential causes of nephrotic syndrome, but are less likely given the biopsy findings described in the scenario. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis typically shows segmental glomerular scarring on biopsy, while membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial immune complex deposits. IgA nephropathy typically shows mesangial hypercellularity and IgA immune complex deposits. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and is responsible for around 20% of cases in adults. It is characterized by normal appearing glomeruli on light microscopy, but diffuse effacement of the podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. The effacement of foot processes results in increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier, leading to significant proteinuria. Incorrect Options: Option A- Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: FSGS is a type of glomerular disease that is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It is characterised by segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis of the glomeruli, meaning that certain parts of the glomerulus are scarred and damaged. On kidney biopsy, FSGS typically shows segmental areas of sclerosis and adhesions between the glomerular tuft and Bowman's capsule. The electron microscopy findings may reveal focal foot process effacement, but this is not as diffuse as that seen in minimal change disease. In this scenario, the biopsy findings are more consistent with minimal change disease than FSGS. Option C- Membranous nephropathy: Membranous nephropathy is a type of glomerulonephritis that is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It is characterised by subepithelial immune complex deposits in the glomerular basement membrane, leading to thickening of the membrane and decreased filtration function. On kidney biopsy, membranous nephropathy typically shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, along with subepithelial immune complex deposits. This is in contrast to the findings seen in this scenario, which are more suggestive of minimal change disease. Option D- IgA nephropathy: IgA nephropathy is a type of glomerulonephritis characterized by mesangial hypercellularity and the deposition of IgA immune complexes in the mesangial region of the glomeruli. It can present with a wide range of clinical symptoms and may progress to chronic kidney disease. On kidney biopsy, IgA nephropathy typically shows mesangial hypercellularity and IgA immune complex deposits. This is not consistent with the findings seen in this scenario, which are more suggestive of minimal change disease. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 33-year-old male presents with a week of progressive, bilateral lower extremity numbness and paresthesias. These symptoms started in his feet, moved to his thighs, and have been associated with weakness over this same period. His past medical history is only significant for Hashimoto thyroiditis and an episode of bloody diarrhea several weeks ago. Physical examination shows 4/5 strength, diminished sensation, and 1+ reflexes in both legs. A nerve conduction study is performed and shows a marked reduction in conduction velocity, prolonged distal motor latency, but minimally reduced amplitude. Which structural element is primarily causing this patient’s symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 33-year-old male presents with a week of progressive, bilateral lower extremity numbness and paresthesias. These symptoms started in his feet, moved to his thighs, and have been associated with weakness over this same period. His past medical history is only significant for Hashimoto thyroiditis and an episode of bloody diarrhea several weeks ago. Physical examination shows 4/5 strength, diminished sensation, and 1+ reflexes in both legs. A nerve conduction study is performed and shows a marked reduction in conduction velocity, prolonged distal motor latency, but minimally reduced amplitude. Which structural element is primarily causing this patient’s symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Schwann cells: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) involves progressive demyelination of the peripheral nervous system . Schwann cells produce the myelin sheath in the peripheral nervous system. GBS frequently occurs following inflammatory, bloody diarrhea due to Campylobacter jejuni and is more common in patients with pre-existing autoimmune diseases. The clinical presentation involves progressive sensory deficits and weakness, usually beginning in the lower extremities in a stocking-and-glove distribution as it moves toward the upper extremities. Physical examination indicates peripheral nerve deficits, including hyporeflexia. The diagnosis is assisted by lumbar puncture demonstrating albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein with a normal white blood cell count) and a nerve conduction study (NCS). NCS and needle electromyography evaluate the electrical properties of peripheral nerves with externally applied stimuli and analysis of the subsequent neurologic response. Recordings can help differentiate between primary nerve and muscle disorders and delineate the site of neuronal dysfunction. NCS results consistent with myelin degeneration (as in GBS) show markedly slowed conduction velocities or absent responses, as well as prolonged distal motor latency, since myelin allows the rapid transmission of action potentials along the axon. Conduction abnormalities progress over time, so serial NCS testing may be useful. Incorrect Options: Option A - Oligodendrocytes: Oligodendrocytes provide the myelin sheath for axons in the central nervous system (CNS). Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating process that occurs in the CNS, but NCS does not have a role in diagnosis of that disease. Option C - Axon: NCS consistent with axonal degeneration would result in a reduced amplitude and an increased dispersion. Velocity may be minimally reduced but not to the degree of myelin degeneration. Option D - Skeletal muscle fibers: NCS of myopathies varies but typically reveals decreased amplitudes. Conduction velocity is not affected. @Neet_pg_bot

He has great difficulty on standard Snellen visual acuity testing with about 20/100 vision in both eyes. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Right homonymous hemianopia: This question stem represents a typical presentation of alexia without agraphia (AWOA) (inability to read without inability to write). This is a disconnection syndrome whereby the visual system and the verbal system are disconnected typically due to a lesion (most commonly a stroke of the posterior cerebral artery) leading to dysfunction of the splenium of the corpus callosum and the left occipital lobe primary visual cortex. In the normal brain visual information from the right occipital lobe is conveyed through the posterior portion of the corpus callosum (the splenium) to the left (dominant hemisphere) angular gyrus of the parietal lobe where that information is processed (along with information from the left occipital lobe). In the event of a destructive lesion of the corpus callosum and the left primary visual cortex, visual information from the left hemifield in both eyes is not recognized because of the corpus callosum dysfunction AND information from the right hemifield in both eyes is not recognized because of destruction of the left occipital lobe primary visual cortex. Thus patients have a dense right homonymous hemianopia on visual field testing and have an inability to effectively process complex visual targets from the left hemifields in both eyes. Because the language centers of the brain are intact in AWOA, these patients are able to comprehend and formulate vocal language without difficulty. Incorrect Options: Option B - Left homonymous hemianopia: This option is incorrect because left homonymous hemianopia would result in loss of the left visual field in both eyes, which would not explain the patient's difficulty with reading a simple sentence aloud. In left homonymous hemianopia, the patient would have intact right visual field vision and should be able to read a simple sentence aloud without difficulty. Option C - Bitemporal hemianopia: Bitemporal hemianopic defects localize to a pathology of the optic chiasm. A left homonymous hemianopia is possible in association with AWOA if patients are right hemisphere dominant but this is exceptionally rare. Binasal defects are not localizable to one lesion and are essentially always associated with either bilateral retinal pathology or bilateral anterior optic nerve pathology (glaucoma is the most common cause by far). Option D - Binasal hemianopia: This option is incorrect because binasal hemianopia is also typically caused by lesions at the level of the optic chiasm, resulting in loss of vision in the inner (nasal) visual fields of both eyes. Similar to bitemporal hemianopia, binasal hemianopia would not explain the patient's difficulty with reading a simple sentence aloud. Option E - Visual field defects are not expected in this setting: This option is incorrect because the patient's symptoms, including difficulty reading a simple sentence aloud and reduced visual acuity, suggest the presence of a visual field defect. Visual field defects can occur in the context of strokes or other neurological conditions that affect the visual pathways or visual cortex. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Acute exacerbation: Acute exacerbation of asthma is a sudden and severe worsening of asthma symptoms, which can be life-threatening. It can be triggered by various factors such as exposure to allergens, infections, exercise, emotional stress, and medication non-adherence. The symptoms of acute exacerbation of asthma may include wheezing, shortness of breath, coughing, chest tightness, and difficulty in breathing. During an acute exacerbation, the airways become inflamed, swollen, and narrowed, making it difficult for air to move in and out of the lungs. This can result in a decrease in oxygen saturation and a rise in carbon dioxide levels in the blood, leading to respiratory failure in severe cases. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pneumonia: While patients with asthma may be at increased risk for developing pneumonia, the scenario does not provide any indication that the patient has an infection or signs of pneumonia on examination. Option B - Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism is a life-threatening condition that can cause shortness of breath, chest pain, and cough, but it is not a common complication of asthma and is unlikely to be the cause of the patient's symptoms based on the scenario. Option D - Bronchitis: Bronchitis is a respiratory condition that is characterized by inflammation of the bronchial tubes and can cause cough, chest discomfort, and shortness of breath. questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the emergency room because of severe chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis that started 30 minutes ago. Her blood pressure is 90/60mmHg, and her pulse rate is 55/min. Past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. An ECG reveals ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), and the patient has been managed accordingly. Angiography reveals right dominant circulation. A few hours later, the telemetry strip reveals a second-degree Mobitz type 1 heart block. What would be the most likely finding on the initial ECG?
questions.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman comes to the emergency room because of severe chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis that started 30 minutes ago. Her blood pressure is 90/60mmHg, and her pulse rate is 55/min. Past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. An ECG reveals ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), and the patient has been managed accordingly. Angiography reveals right dominant circulation. A few hours later, the telemetry strip reveals a second-degree Mobitz type 1 heart block. What would be the most likely finding on the initial ECG?

options.label: A
options.text: ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL

options.label: B
options.text: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF

options.label: D
options.text: Diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR depression

questions.answerText: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF
questions.solution: Correct Option B- ST-segment elevation in leads II III aVF: This patient’s bradycardia on initial presentation and a second-degree heart block later on suggests inferior wall myocardial infarction. Inferior wall MI will present as ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. The branches of the right coronary artery supply the inferior wall of the heart. The posterior descending artery (PDA) supplies the AV node and arises from the RCA in 90% of the cases (right dominant circulation). Infraction of the inferior wall will result in systolic dysfunction of the right ventricle , resulting in decreased preload into the left ventricle and hence a fall in the cardiac output. Therefore a patient who develops a second-degree heart block after myocardial infarction has undergone an inferior wall infarction in the majority of cases. AV block due to MI will resolve in 8-10 days . In symptomatic patients following options are available: IV Atropine (0.6mg) Temporary pacemaker Incorrect Options: Option A- ST-segment elevation in leads I aVL: ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL represents lateral wall MI. The left circumflex artery (LCX) supplies the heart's lateral wall. The posterior descending artery will arise from LCX in less than 10% of the cases (left dominant circulation). This patient’s angiography revealed a right dominant circulation, so he likely suffered from an inferior wall MI. Option C- Sawtooth appearance of waves: Atrial flutter is characterized by a large re-entry circuit near the cavotricuspid isthmus in the right atrium. The atrial rate is usually 300/min. ECG will show a characteristic sawtooth appearance of the flutter waves. Treatment options include: Catheter ablation Rate control by digoxin, β-blockers, or verapamil. Rhythm control using DC cardioversion. Anticoagulation according to the CHA2DS2-VASc scoring system. Option D- Diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR depression: Acute pericarditis results from the inflammation of the pericardium and is characterized by diffuse ST-segment elevation and/or PR depression. The typical presentation is a retrosternal chest pain that radiates to the neck and shoulders, aggravated by breathing and relieved by leaning forward . Fever is also common. Some of the important causes include the following: Viral infection Malignancy Systemic lupus erythematosus Uremia Myocardial infarction ECG findings include: Widespread ST elevation with upward concavity PR depression T wave inversion may be found after some time Treatment options include: NSAIDs Colchicine Glucocorticoids Pericardiocentesis in case of large effusions. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male comes to the emergency department due to acute left leg pain for the past 30 minutes. He says that he was at home watching TV when the pain occurred suddenly and severely. His medical history is significant for hypertension, however, he is not compliant with his prescribed medicines. Physical examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse, a pale leg, an absent left popliteal pulse, and decreased sensation to pin prick. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male comes to the emergency department due to acute left leg pain for the past 30 minutes. He says that he was at home watching TV when the pain occurred suddenly and severely. His medical history is significant for hypertension, however, he is not compliant with his prescribed medicines. Physical examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse, a pale leg, an absent left popliteal pulse, and decreased sensation to pin prick. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Atrial fibrillation: This patient’s presentation with acute leg pain, pulselessness, pallor, and paresthesia is suggestive of acute limb ischemia secondary to thromboembolism. An irregularly irregular pulse along with a presentation of acute limb ischemia is consistent with atrial fibrillation Pathogenesis of A-fib is characterized by abnormal automatic firing and the presence of multiple interacting reentry circuits looping around the atria . Episodes of AF are initiated by rapid bursts of ectopic beats arising from conducting tissue in the pulmonary veins or from diseased/dilated atrial tissue. Atrial fibrillation most commonly occurs due to atrial remodeling as a result of hypertension (as in this patient) and other cardiac disorders e.g. mitral stenosis. Atrial fibrillation results in stasis of blood flow in the left atrium . As a result, there is an increased risk of thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage. This thrombus can subsequently embolize into the systemic circulation and lead to ischemia of the affected region. Incorrect Options: Option B- Atherosclerosis: Atherosclerosis is a chronic process characterized by the accumulation of cholesterol plaques in the arteries which leads to a reduction in blood flow. It can lead to chronic limb ischemia rather than acute limb ischemia. Chronic limb ischemia presents with limb claudication and diminished pulses. Option C- Compartment syndrome: Compartment syndrome is characterized by increased pressure within a muscle compartment , leading to decreased blood flow and subsequent damage to nerves and muscles It most commonly occurs as a result of traumatic limb fractures This patient with an irregular pulse and no history of trauma is most likely suffering from A-fib Option D- Deep Vein Thrombosis: DVT presents with pain and swelling of the leg rather than pulselessness and pallor. It usually occurs in a hypercoagulable state e.g. pregnancy and reduced mobility e.g. after surgery This patient with an irregular pulse and acute limb ischemia is most likely suffering from A-fib @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which phase of the cell cycle is most variable in length of time?
questions.stemHtml: Which phase of the cell cycle is most variable in length of time?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - G1 Phase The G1 phase is highly variable in length, whereas the M, S, and G2 phases do not vary much. The cell cycle is a series of stages through which cells progress in the process of duplication of its DNA and division into two daughter cells. It is made up of 4 phases: G1, S phase, G2, and M phase. In order to progress to the next phase, the preceding phase must be completed. The cell cycle is regulated by proteins called cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs). Cyclins will bind to CDKs to activate them as a signal to progress through the cell cycle. Cells may leave the cell cycle and enter the G0 phase when they have stopped dividing. Lastly, the combination of phases where the cell is NOT in the M phase (G1, S phase and G2) is collectively known as Interphase. Incorrect Options: Option B - G2 Phase: The G2 phase is a relatively short phase of the cell cycle and is not as variable in length as the G1 phase. During the G2 phase, the cell continues to grow and prepare for mitosis (M phase). It is a critical phase where the cell checks for any errors or damage in DNA replication during the S phase. Once the cell completes the G2 phase, it proceeds to the M phase to undergo cell division. Option C - M Phase: The M phase, also known as mitosis, is a relatively short and highly regulated phase of the cell cycle. It involves the actual process of cell division, including the segregation of duplicated chromosomes and the splitting of the cell into two daughter cells. The duration of the M phase is relatively consistent and does not show significant variability compared to the G1 phase. Option D - S Phase: The S phase is the phase of the cell cycle where DNA synthesis and replication occur. During this phase, the cell's genetic material is duplicated to prepare for cell division. The duration of the S phase is relatively consistent in most cells and is essential for accurate transmission of genetic information to daughter cells. While the S phase may vary slightly between different cell types, it is not as variable in length as the G1 phase. @Neet_pg_bot

No mucosal irregularities are seen, but four-quadrant biopsies are obtained of the 2.5 Barrett's segment. Dysplasia is noted on several of the histologic specimens. Which of the following is the next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 61-year-old male with longstanding GERD and a history of Barrett’s esophagus undergoes surveillance endoscopy. No mucosal irregularities are seen, but four-quadrant biopsies are obtained of the 2.5 Barrett's segment. Dysplasia is noted on several of the histologic specimens. Which of the following is the next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: He should continue to undergo surveillance endoscopy to see if this develops into carcinoma.

options.label: B
options.text: He should undergo radiofrequency ablation therapy.

options.label: D
options.text: He should undergo endoscopic mucosal resection

questions.answerText: He should undergo endoscopic mucosal resection
questions.solution: Correct Option D - He should undergo endoscopic mucosal resection: The next step in management in a patient with Barrett's esophagus who is found to have dysplasia within a "short" (<3 cm) Barrett's segment or intramucosal carcinoma in a biopsy, is to perform staging studies (further biopsies, generally at every 1 cm), followed by endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR). Incorrect Options: Option A - He should continue to undergo surveillance endoscopy to see if this develops into carcinoma: This option is incorrect because dysplasia in Barrett's esophagus is considered a precancerous condition. When dysplasia is identified, it indicates an increased risk of developing esophageal carcinoma (cancer). As such, continued surveillance is not the appropriate course of action. Intervention is required to prevent the progression to carcinoma. Option B - He should undergo radiofrequency ablation therapy: This option is incorrect because radiofrequency ablation (RFA) therapy is typically used for the treatment of Barrett's esophagus with low-grade dysplasia or high-grade dysplasia that does not involve any visible cancer (carcinoma in situ). In this case, the patient has dysplasia on several histologic specimens, which may indicate a more advanced stage than what RFA can address. Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or other treatments might be more suitable. Option C - He should undergo photodynamic therapy: This option is incorrect because photodynamic therapy (PDT) is used for treating high-grade dysplasia or early-stage esophageal carcinoma that is limited to the superficial layers of the esophagus (also known as intramucosal carcinoma). In this case, the patient has dysplasia but no visible mucosal irregularities, which suggests that PDT may not be the most appropriate treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements describes the role that hiatal hernias play in the pathogenesis of GERD?

options.label: A
options.text: The size of a sliding hiatal hernia does not correlate with the degree of impact it has on the pathogenesis of GERD.

options.label: B
options.text: A sliding hiatal hernia is associated with a proximally displaced LES, resulting in a decrease in LES pressure as well as loss of function as a valve.

options.label: C
options.text: Patients with hiatal hernias do not have an increased incidence of transient esophageal relaxations.

options.label: D
options.text: A hiatal hernia does not result in changes to the structure of the esophagus that impede acid clearance.

questions.answerText: A sliding hiatal hernia is associated with a proximally displaced LES, resulting in a decrease in LES pressure as well as loss of function as a valve.
questions.solution: Correct Option B - A hiatal hernia does not result in changes to the structure of the esophagus that impede acid clearance: The impact that a sliding hiatal hernia has in the pathogenesis of GERD is in relation to increasing size of the sliding hiatal hernia. A sliding hiatal hernia is associated with a proximally displaced LES, resulting in a decrease in LES pressure in proportion to the size of the hiatal hernia, as well as a loss of LES function as a valve when it is in the intra-abdominal position, allowing a larger refluxate to be regurgitated into the esophagus. Additionally, studies have noted a greater incidence of transient esophageal relaxations in patients with sliding hiatal hernias. Incorrect Options: Option A - The size of a sliding hiatal hernia does not correlate with the degree of impact it has on the pathogenesis of GERD: The size of a sliding hiatal hernia can indeed have an impact on the severity of GERD symptoms and its pathogenesis. Larger hiatal hernias may allow for more significant reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus, leading to more severe symptoms. In some cases, larger hernias can also affect the position and function of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), contributing to GERD. Option C - Patients with hiatal hernias do not have an increased incidence of transient esophageal relaxations: Hiatal hernias are associated with an increased incidence of transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations (TLESRs). TLESRs are one of the main mechanisms that allow stomach contents to reflux into the esophagus. In patients with hiatal hernias, the herniated part of the stomach may mechanically disrupt the normal anti-reflux barrier and contribute to the occurrence of TLESRs, leading to GERD. Option D - A hiatal hernia does not result in changes to the structure of the esophagus that impede acid clearance: Hiatal hernias can indeed cause structural changes in the esophagus that impede acid clearance. The presence of a hiatal hernia alters the normal anatomy of the gastroesophageal junction, which can impair the ability of the esophagus to clear acid and other stomach contents effectively. This impaired acid clearance can worsen GERD symptoms and contribute to esophagitis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - EPd Given that the patient has shown progression after enjoying 22 months of progression-free survival (PFS) with DRd (Daratumumab, Lenalidomide, Dexamethasone), the most appropriate next treatment option would be an elotuzumab (E) combination. Elotuzumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets SLAMF7 on myeloma cells and natural killer cells, promoting myeloma cell death through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). It is approved for use in combination with pomalidomide (P) and dexamethasone (d) for patients who have received at least two prior therapies, including lenalidomide and a proteasome inhibitor. Option D - Ed+ melphalan: The option "Ed+ melphalan" is not a recognized or approved treatment regimen for multiple myeloma. questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a past medical history significant for hypertension presents to the clinic with complaints of persistent headaches, muscle weakness, and fatigue. He reports taking his medications regularly, including lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. His blood pressure is 170/110 mmHg, and his heart rate is 90 beats/min. His laboratory results show low serum potassium levels, with a value of 2.7 mEq/L. The patient undergoes further evaluation, which reveals a diagnosis of bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male with a past medical history significant for hypertension presents to the clinic with complaints of persistent headaches, muscle weakness, and fatigue. He reports taking his medications regularly, including lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. His blood pressure is 170/110 mmHg, and his heart rate is 90 beats/min. His laboratory results show low serum potassium levels, with a value of 2.7 mEq/L. The patient undergoes further evaluation, which reveals a diagnosis of bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Spironolactone: The most appropriate treatment for bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is spironolactone. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is a condition characterized by the enlargement of both adrenal glands, leading to the overproduction of aldosterone, which is responsible for sodium retention and potassium loss, leading to hypertension and hypokalemia, respectively. Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist that competitively inhibits the binding of aldosterone to its receptor, leading to increased excretion of sodium and retention of potassium, ultimately resulting in a reduction in blood pressure and restoration of potassium levels. Incorrect Options: Option B - Metolazone: Metolazone is a thiazide-like diuretic that inhibits the reabsorption of sodium and chloride in the distal convoluted tubules. Although metolazone may help reduce blood pressure in some patients, it does not specifically address the underlying cause of bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, which is the overproduction of aldosterone. Option C - Dexamethasone: Dexamethasone is a synthetic corticosteroid that has potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects. It is used to treat a wide range of conditions, including autoimmune disorders, allergies, and cancer. However, dexamethasone does not specifically address the overproduction of aldosterone in bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Option D - Hydrocortisone: Hydrocortisone is a synthetic corticosteroid that is commonly used to treat various endocrine and autoimmune disorders. However, it does not specifically address the overproduction of aldosterone in bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. @Neet_pg_bot
